english: Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act
spanish: Ley de Antiterrorismo y de una Pena de Muerte Efectiva
comments: The 'death penalty' part of this refers to provisions for the death penalty in the use of plastic explosives, as well as in the killing or attempted killing of multiple people. (https://www.congress.gov/104/plaws/publ132/PLAW-104publ132.htm) The term 'effective' has a few potential meanings, primarily A) in effect, as in, vigente, B) having the desired effect, efectivo, as well as C) having the end result of despite it not being specifically provided for, which would be something like realor actual. At no point in the above-cited legal text is the term effective, in fact, defined in the way it is used in the title of the law. Are we creating an "effective death penalty" despite the absence of a death penalty, or are we creating a "death penalty" that is more effective, as in, actually results in deaths of those convicted of the corresponding qualifying crimes? It would appear that we are, in fact, referring to the latter -- as the law provides for the death penalty in more cases than previously, and strips away some (apparently many) habeas corpus protections previously available. Therefore, a literal translation is justified -- Ley de Antiterrorismo y de una Pena de Muerte Efectiva.

comments: "recurrir" is technically the generic, un-marked equivalent in Spanish for "appeal" in English. However, "recursos" include a number of remedies that, in English, would be equivalent to "motions to reconsider" -- a request for reconsideration that does not go to a higher court. In English, "appeal" implies, if not necessarily requires, that the same be to a court of higher instance. Moreover, in the Immigration context, all appeals are, in fact, to a court of higher instance (although maybe, once a case has been successfully appealed at the BIA and remanded to the EOIR for further hearings, this might in fact be a "recurso"); thus, virtually whenever we are discussing appeals in the EOIR, it would be appropriate to talk about "apelaciones", which would be most accurately translated as "appeals to a court of higher instance". Of course, "recurrir" is *also* correct, but could be considered higher or more technical in its register, and perhaps should not be recommended due to that reason. See specifically Jowers, 164 and 168.

spanish: abogado que consta en el expediente; abogado representante; abogado oficial
comments: Jowers provides interesting options regarding this concept in Spain, where often one employs two attorneys: one, a procurador, represents their client before a court in all pre-trial and administrative tasks; and the abogado or letrado who defends the client in court--in trial settings, for example. In other words, one specializes in procedural and paperwork issues, the other in oral argument and litigation (Jowers, 97). While interesting, this usage of procurador would be very confusing in the context of other countries' legal systems, where it may mean something more like prosecutor. There are additional uses, in Spain, Venezuela and elsewhere, of apoderado, but as this may come back into English as agent, among other uses, it is not appropriate here, either. Many law offices and agencies in the US like to use 'abogado oficial' for this phrase, but often in EOIR proceedings, it is heard when explaining that an attorney does, or does not, represent a respondent for a particular proceeding. For example, 'That's correct, ma'am, Atty Fulano is the attorney of record in your bond proceedings, but not in this, your immigration proceeding'. It may well be helpful to use a more explanatory translations in such situations.

En España, se habla de 'actos de comunicación', 'comunicaciones' en general, y más específicamente, 'notificaciones, citaciones y emplazamientos'. Parece ser que el aviso inicial de un caso en contra de uno (el clásico 'you've been served') es la notificación; luego vienen citaciones y emplazamientos. Dandole otra vuelta, en Alcaraz: "dar traslado a: give notice, serve notice, pass on a notification (...) Los litigantes tienen la obligación de dar traslado a la parte contraria copias de las pruebas que van a aportar en el juicio;" En resumen: Si conoces el contexto cultural, y crees que puedes acertar con el término correcto para tal cultura, adelante. spanish: (Immigration Court in general) Tribunal de lo migratorio; (the building) el Tribunal; (the courtroom) la sala, esta sala; (the Judge) yo, el/la juez
comments: It would appear (RAE, entre otros) that a 'juzgado' refers to an adjudicatory body consisting of a single judicial officer who hears cases at the first-instance level. A 'tribunal' or a 'corte', however, generally refer to multi-judge panels, or at least, second-instance level adjudicatory bodies. Therefore, we should be referring to Immigration Court at least as a 'corte' or 'tribunal'. However, the EOIR is not, strictly speaking, a court; the IJs are not judges, after all. The EOIR is a body which conducts administrative hearings, and the bulk of the law by and through which it makes its decisions is administrative law. In fact, the EOIR is, in many ways, closest to what in some Hispanic countries (Uruguay, Mexico, Spain) is known as the Tribunal de lo Contencioso-Administrativo, which is a jurisdiction that in general hears cases de novo arising from disputes with the public institutions of the country. Now, the EOIR hears many cases on what you could consider a first instance basis, pursuant to the issuance of an NTA. This fits with the viewpoint of the contencioso-administrativo; the Respondent sought or is seeking admission to the country, in essence they were denied this service, and as a result there is a dispute which needs to be settled. There are, of course, many cases that the EOIR hears which are referred or transferred from USCIS, frequently with an initial denial from USCIS. This fits even more closely with the traditional profile of the contencioso-administrativo, in the sense that the individual requested a service from the public administration (asylum, adjustment of status, etc.), and this service was not provided to them -- or, the result of that service was not what they desired -- and now they seek a remedy through a body designed to hear such disputes. Based on this, the recommendation is that the EOIR be referred to not as a 'corte', but rather as a 'tribunal', in accordance with the widespread usage of this term to denote the contencioso-administrativo adjudicatory bodies in multiple countries.
source: Refactor_ EOIR Spanish-English Glossary 2020.xlsx - 2020 Terms List.csv

comments: It would appear that there is not a strong tendency towards universal naturalization and citizenship processes from one country to another, especially as regards the categorization of these processes. In the US we might talk about 'acquired' versus 'derivative' citizenthip; Mexico's main categories appear to be 'por nacimiento' and 'por naturalización', simple enough; both Spain and Guatemala have ciudadanía 'de orígen' (US' 'acquired'), but Spain also has 'recuperada', 'por opción', and 'por residencia'. None of those three countries has something that specifically appears to correspond to 'derivative' citizenship/naturalization. And whereas the concept of 'derivative' naturalization and 'derivative' status are corollaries in English, explaining naturalization as 'derivada' isn't particularly helpful or representative of the meaning of the English. In the context of 'derivative status', it's generally quite clear what's meant: the lead has the main case, the riders the secondary cases, and the riders are therefore derived from the lead. Hence I propose this solution for 'derivative citizenship', and a very different solution for 'derivative status'. Of course, if there is a better solution out there, it should be adopted! See 'Nationality and Status' reference for more.

spanish: gran jurado; jurado indagatorio, acusatorio; jurado de instrucción
comments: The concept of a 'grand jury' is one that pertains to Anglo-Saxon common law. As such, various renderings are possible that express the concept to varying degrees of clarity depending on the target dialect or region. The 'jury' part of the phrase is most certainly 'jurado'; 'gran jurado' may well be an adequate choice, given that the phrase in English, "grand jury", is at this point a term of art that does not have an inherent meaning unless the listener has previously learned and understood it. 'jurado indagatorio' or 'jurado acusatorio' may well be good middle-of-the-road options, which provide a certain amount of explaining, are dialect neutral, and offer two distinct levels of register. If, however, you are sure of the listener's geographical dialect, you could opt for 'jurado de instrucción' if the listener is from any number of countries which still employs (or employed in the recent past) the figure of jueces de instrucción-- for example, Colombia, Ecuador, Spain, Bolivia, or Mexico (as per the Criminal Codes of each one of those respective nations).

comments: Black's: "A court order commanding or preventing an action." A reading of entries in Ossorio regarding interdicto gives the clear impression that this term refers to injunctions issued specifically regarding property disputes, and doesn't appear to be more broadly applicable. Ossorio, "Auto: ...En general se puede decir que, mientras la providencia afecta a cuestiones de mero trámite y la sentencia pone fin a la instancia o al juicio criminal, el auto resuelve cuestiones de fondo que se plantean antes de la sentencia." In other words, any sort of finding or order that the judge makes before the sentencing or final decision period; this is too broad for the more specific meaning of injunction. A reading of entries regarding mandato in Ossorio shows that this term clearly corresponds to the English mandate. Ossorio de nuevo, "Mandamiento: Orden que un juez o tribunal dicta, dentro de sus facultades, para que sea cumplida una decisión o se haga eficaz un acto procesal. En ese sentido se habla de mandamiento de pago, de embargo, de desalojo, etc." This sounds close, although 'mandamiento judicial' has a highly specific meaning in Spanish civil law, again regarding property. However, "Requerimiento: Acto judicial por el que se intima a alguien para que haga o deje de hacer una cosa. | Es también el aviso, manifestación o pregunta que se hace, generalmente bajo fe notarial, a alguna persona, exigiendo o buscando de ella que exprese y declare su actitud o su respuesta. Ofrece, pues, gran importancia en el Derecho Procesal." Note that the second meaning of requerimiento is a specific one, referring essentially to subpoena powers (this usage also appears in broad use in the Spanish criminal code, for example) and could cause confusion depending on the context.

comments: Keep in mind the subtleties of 'recurso' and 'apelación'. A 'recurso de apelación' is, by definition, an appeal to a court of higher instance; 'apelación' on its own is an elliptical reference to the same concept, and 'recurso', being the broader category, can also include 'recurso de apelación' in an elliptical sense. However, 'recursos' can also include what we would call in English 'motions to reconsider'; if an 'interlocutory appeal' is being discussed, it is by definition to a court of higher instance; if it isn't to a court of higher instance, it is more properly a motion to reconsider. https://legislacion.vlex.es/vid/ley-enjuiciamiento-civil-126688 Also, consider Ossorio's entry for 'Auto interlocutorio': "El que no afecta a lo principal de una causa, por dictarse en un incidente o artículo de previo pronunciamiento. (v. AUTO DEFINITIVO)." This corresponds quite clearly to, in Black's, both interlocutory injunction, which reroutes to preliminary injunction: "A temporary injunction issued before or during trial to prevent an irreparable injury from occurring before the court has a chance to decide the case..."

Thus, for example, if an IJ is explaining, "Your application is currently before USCIS, I don't have jurisdiction," or "Your case is still before a different Immigration Court, a COV hasn't been granted, I don't have jurisdiction," it would be appropriate in Spanish to say no soy la juez competente or no tengo competencia rather than no tengo jurisdicción, as jurisdicción refers in its most specific meaning to the ability of the Judge to apply the law to the facts of a case. spanish: (enforce or carry out the law) aplicar, cumplir con la ley; (ensure compliance with the law) hacer cumplir, cumplir con la ley; (police) la policía; (other law enforcement bodies in general) la autoridad, las autoridades; (the justice system) la justicia; (generic concept of legality and societal order) orden público
comments: Etymologically speaking, 'enforce' is Latin, or at least has Latin roots, but originated either in Middle Ages French or Renaissance English, and was being used in the sense of 'ensure compliance with a law' as of the mid-1600s. Thus, though intuition would say that there must be a common root somewhere, the meaning of 'fuerza' and 'forzar' are far separated from the English meaning in this context, being far more physical in their connotative usage. 'enforce' is also a transitive verb, a situation which is not easily mirrored, either, in Spanish. Further complicating the issue is the broad euphemistic or metonymical usage of 'law enforcement' in English. As a blanket term, it is used to refer to any sort of body or agency which uses legally sanctioned force to ensure compliance with the law. Given English's syntactic flexibility, this presents the translator or interpreter frequently with the struggle of having to construct a significantly different sentence or work-around in Spanish in order to adequately express the English. Keep in mind as well the almost-homonymical phrase 'in force', which corresponds to 'en vigor'.

spanish: examen de recursos económicos; prueba, comprobación de medios
comments: A 'means test' is an examination of economic/financial resources carried out in order to determine whether someone qualifies to receive government assistance, whether disbursement for a specific purpose or in general. As per 8 CFR § 213a.1 - Definitions, it is defined as: "Means-tested public benefit means either a Federal means-tested public benefit, which is any public benefit funded in whole or in part by funds provided by the Federal Government that the Federal agency administering the Federal funds has determined to be a Federal means-tested public benefit under the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996, Public Law 104-193, or a State means-tested public benefit, which is any public benefit for which no Federal funds are provided that a State, State agency, or political subdivision of a State has determined to be a means-tested public benefit. No benefit shall be considered to be a means-tested public benefit if it is a benefit described in sections 401(b), 411(b), 422(b) or 423(d) of Public Law 104-193." In itself, it is a term used in more 'meta' contexts--social science or policy documents, for example. This is borne out in Spanish as well as English, with most government websites describing public assistance talking about 'requisitos para percibir ayudas'. A fairly reliable source, a Guía práctica para responsabilidades de expedientes relativos al convenio de cobro de alimentos para los hijos de 2007 published by the Hague Conference on Private International Law, refers to this as "examen de recursos económicos". In a lack of an overwhelming consensus on the term, however, other options are not objectionable.

spanish: definitivamente/no definitivamente; firme/no firme; con fuerza de cosa juzgada/sin fuerza de cosa juzgada
comments: Prejudice is one of those terms that legal intepreters and translators love to fight over. This is the situation: In English, we have these two terms, 'with' and 'without prejudice', and they mean, essentially, that (in general) the same charges or case could, or could not, be filed again. Interestingly, this meaning of prejudice, while used in Black's, is not defined. This is related to the concept of res judicata, also known as cosa juzgada, which Black's gives as "1. An issue that has been definitively settled by judicial decision. 2. An affirmative defense barring the same parties from litigating a second lawsuit on the same claim, or any other claim arising from the same transaction or series of transactions and that could have been--but was not--raised in the first suit." That second definition is the meaning given by Black's for prejudice. So while the concepts are almost identical, their usage is not. In addition, there is, in Spanish, the concept of firme, defined by the DEJ of the RAE as, "Adm. y Proc. Dicho de un acto o resolución administrativa o judicial: Invariable, por no haber sido impugnado o no admitir recurso." Frequently, this is used to express whether a sentence is firme o no.  In a way, this is a good thing for us translators and interpreters--it gives us power to decide how we want to express the concept. The flip side to this is that we need to understand the different concepts and deploy them properly. This particular usage--'the application has been withdrawn with prejudice'--could, for example, be rendered as se ha retirado la solicitud definitivamente,  or perhaps se ha retirado la solicitud de manera firme, but definitely not se ha retirado la solicitud con fuerza de cosa juzgada, because after all, a decision has not been made about the application. If it were regarding a criminal case, or even an individual hearing on an application for relief, our options are different. For additional consideration, see entries on 'sobreseimiento' and 'desestimación' in the 'Decisions and Appeals' reference.

spanish: (US Immigration rules) Carga Pública; carga al público, carga para la asistencia social
comments: The United States has long had a history (since the 19th century) of rules in immigration designed to eliminate or discourage the entry of immigrants who could become a burden to society, that is, a public charge. 'burden' is translated as 'carga' (onus probandi should be left in Latin), and charge, here, is a bit of an antiquated usage that refers to what is more commonly called being a ward, commonly heard in Juvenile or Family law contexts in the phrase ward of the state, which could be rendered as pupilo del Estado. Using 'pupilo' for 'public charge' would be an over-translation, choosing a term that is more specific than what is meant: carga is an appropriate equivalent for both burden and charge. There is extensive usage of 'carga pública' to refer to these US rules, from USCIS to immigration advocacy groups to press coverage in Mexico and Spain. ( https://www.uscis.gov/es/tarjeta-verde/carga-publica )This concept of immigrants being a burden exists in Spain; searches on the topic in Mexico revealed programs designed to support migrants, rather than exclude them. Spain's phrasing is, "...para no convertirse en una carga para la asistencia social en España durante su periodo de residencia..." (emphasis added). http://extranjeros.mitramiss.gob.es/es/InformacionInteres/InformacionProcedimientos/CiudadanosComunitarios/hoja102/index.html#aplicacion

INS, Mr. Elramly had been convicted of a 'serious drug offense', and therefore had to show the BIA 'unusual or outstanding and countervailing equities' that would overcome the serious drug offense on his record. There are a few complicating factors: 'equities' should, linguistically, be positive factors. However, in Immigration law they are often 'negative or positive equities', in other words, negative or positive factors to be balanced. 'outstanding' can mean 'really exceptional', and it can also mean 'still in existence'.  'countervailing', meanwhile, is a term that means 'to be worth as much as'. So what we're looking at, here, is 'positive factors that are unusual, exceptional/still in existence and of equal, but opposite, weight.'

comments: The coexistence of 'forum' and 'venue' is a lovely example of the multiple pools that the English language draws from, and of there being two terms in English equating to one in Spanish. Both are, of course, Latin in origin, but venuecame later from French, referring to 'the place to which the case comes' (Black's), and forum, far older, refers more specifically to 'the place of jurisdiction' (Black's). A more in-depth explanation, again Black's, quoting Charles Alan Wright, The Law of Federal Courts, "The distinction must be clearly understood between jurisdiction, which is the power to adjudicate, and venue, which relates to the place where judicial authority may be exercised and is intended for the convenience of the litigants. It is possible for jurisdiction to exist though venue in a particular district is improper, and it is possible for a suit to be brought in the appropriate venue though it must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction." See also jurisdiction, competence.

comments: This is a frequently-used expression which, at least at Cleveland EOIR, we have observed Central American speakers use when they wish to describe what we would describe as a rape, or an attempted rape (see Sex Crimes reference for more on this topic). The dilemma is that, when a speaker simply says, 'El abusó de mí', how far do we go? Do we say simply 'He raped me', or do we use the arguably equivalent 'He took advantage of me', and leave it up to the attorneys to clarify? There is danger in both overstating and in understating. It is clear to us that what is meant is that a sexual act was committed, and likely, one that involved penetration and force (again, see the Sex Crimes reference for why this is particularly pertinent). Based on our experience with the expression and the stories that it is used to tell, as well as the technical definition of 'sexual assault', we recommend 'assault' for this expression: it communicates the force inherent in the expression, while still leaving it vague enough that it should provoke the necessary follow-up questions from counsel.

comments: In a similar way to the discussion surrounding 'abusar de', the moment when a speaker simply says 'me maltrató' can be a delicate one. There is a risk in rendering this as 'he/she mistreated me', and a risk in rendering it as 'he/she abused me'. Something to keep in mind are the long-term effects of any kind of abuse, and the effort that it often times takes for the victim to discuss that abuse later. As interpreters, we are sworn to transparently transfer meaning from one language to another. We also must consider being trauma informed when interpreting issues of trauma, and not to shy away from calling abuse what it is, even when the speaker struggles to call it that. Both 'abuso' and 'maltrato' are used in Spanish, although based on anecdotal evidence, 'maltrato' seems, at least in many dialects, to be a preferential or less English-influenced choice, especially when describing abuse experienced by the speaker.

englishDefinition:
finding. See FINDING OF FACT. finding of fact. comments: For our purposes, 'finding' and 'ruling' should be considered synonyms. See 'ruling' for more. Note that a 'finding' in English frequently is limited in scope; a judge or other fact finder may make a finding regarding a specific issue of fact or law, although it can be used more broadly ("I find you guilty" is technically a specific issue of law, but is often expressed using 'fallo' in Spanish). 'I've made a finding regarding removability', therefore, might more appropriately be a 'decisión', although 'the prebious IJ's finding regarding removability' could easily be 'el fallo del juez de lo migratorio previo en cuanto a la expulsabilidad' would also be appropriate.

ruling, n. (16c) 1. The outcome of a court's decision either on some point oflaw or on the case as a whole. Also termed legal ruling. Cf. JUDGMENT (1); OPINION (1). [Cases: Courts C:";)88.] "A distinction is sometimes made between rules and rulings. Whether or not a formal distinction is declared, in common usage 'legal ruling' (or simply 'ruling') is a term ordinarily used to signify the outcome of applying a legal test when that outcome is one of relatively narrow impact. The immediate effect is to decide an issue in a single case. This meaning contrasts, for example, with the usual meaning of 'legal rule' (or simply 'rule'). The term 'rule' ordinarily refers to a legal proposition of general application. A 'ruling' may have force as precedent, but ordinarily it has that force because the conclusion it
expresses (for example, 'objection sustained') explicitly depends upon and implicitly reiterates a 'rule' a legal proposition of more general application ...." Robert E. Keeton, Judging 67-68 (1990). 2. Parliamentary law. The chair's decision on a point of order. rule, vb.

comments: When an appeal is filed, opposing counsel generally files a motion for dismissal. This is, in many contexts, often referred to as a 'motion for summary judgment', and is often brought during trial, after a party has rested, as a way of pre-empting the remainder of the trial and asking the Judge to make a finding that said party has been unable to sustain their burden. A motion for summary dismissal is slightly different, in that it is made at the very beginning of a process (generally civil, administrative, or appellate), one could say before the process has already begun, and asks the appellate authorities to throw the case out due to legal or factual insufficiency. This is similar, but distinct in an important way, from a process that in Spanish is known as 'inadmisión a trámite'. In Spanish-language jurisdictions, commonly there is someone who has the authority (often a secretario judicial) and responsibility of deciding whether a case is admitted, or not, to the judicial process; this person makes a prima facie decision regarding jurisdiction and legal sufficiency, and either lo admite a trámite or lo inadmita a trámite. However, there is a fundamental difference here, because the person making the decision is the judicial authority itself, it is Court staff making a unilateral decision; a summary dismissal is action taken by the Court at the behest of counsel, already within the adversarial framework.

english: A standard of proof, as per Black's: The degree or level of proof demanded in a specific case, such as "beyond a reasonable doubt" or "by a preponderance of the evidence." See BURDEN OF PERSUASION. This concept is so essential to the Anglo-Saxon understanding of law that it can be difficult to describe it, and to conceive of a judicial system without it. It could perhaps be described as the minimum level by which a case can be considered to be proven, based on the wording of the law (be it statutory or case law). When reading Spanish-language discussions of the concept, you will encounter the term umbral used to describe this idea: a "threshold for proof". While this concept  does not exist as such in civil law countries, it is beginning to be imported, and is frequently described using a very literal phrasing, "estándar de prueba". See, notably, Los estándares de prueba en el proceso penal español, Jordi Ferrer Beltrán, Estándares probatorios en el sistema acusatorio y su desarrollo en Colombia, Claudia Edith Velandia Coy, Aplicación del estándar de prueba por los jueces promiscuos, autores varios.

spanishDefinition:
*CAUSA. A. En general. El motivo que nos mueve o la razón que nos inclina a hacer alguna cosa. También, el antecedente necesario que origina un efecto. Se habla asimismo de causa como fundamento por
el cual adquirimos algún derecho y en este sentido se confunde a veces con el título. B. En Derecho Civil. La causa existe tanto en las obligaciones como en los contratos. Para algunos, es el fin esencial o más
próximo que los contratantes se proponen al contratar. C. En Derecho Romano. Como variedad del Derecho Civil en general, resulta de interés señalar las diferentes acepciones que los romanistas le señalan a esta voz en las fuentes genuinas del mismo: a) motivo o razón personal de un acto jurídico, como metus causa (debido al miedo) o causa donandi (la causa de donar, por un favor recibido, para seducir, etc.); b) el fin
directo e inmediato, como la tradición o entrega, por causa de venta, de pagos; c) acto jurídico o hecho que precede a un negocio jurídico, aunque este matiz no proceda de los jurisconsultos romanos antiguos; d)
elemento accesorio, como la condición, el modo y el plazo en la obligación; e) litigio, proceso; f) negocio jurídico en general; g) situación de hecho que sirve de soporte a una relación jurídica conforme a su destino;
como la causa dotis, permanente, lo mismo que las cargas matrimoniales a cuyo alivio está destinada. D. En Derecho Político. Causa significa el partido o los intereses que se sirven o con los cuales se simpatiza en
una lucha electoral, parlamentaria, ciudadana; también, un bando en una guerra civil o internacional. E. En Derecho Procesal. Contienda judicial; esto es, todo asunto entre partes que se sigue y ventila
contradictoriamente ante un tribunal, en la forma establecida por las leyes, hasta su resolución definitiva. Expediente o proceso que se forma para la substanciación del negocio o cuerpo mismo de los autos.
CIVIL. Litigio ante la jurisdicción ordinaria. CRIMINAL. Juicio ante la jurisdicción penal, para averiguación de los delitos y de sus autores, y aplicar la decisión legal pertinente. ILICITA. La contraria a las
leyes, a la moral o al orden público. LICITA. La ajustada a las leyes, a la moral y al orden público; o, al menos, no prohibida por tales normas. LUCRATIVA. La que posee por título la liberalidad o la beneficencia.
NULA. La que no surte efectos positivos en Derecho, porque vicia el acto esencialmente y lo condena a la ineficacia; salvo confumación o prescripción de la acción contra el mismo. La causa ilícita contra el orden
público y la falsa anulan los negocios jurídicos en que se dan y, más realistamente, donde se descubren y se aducen contra su validez. PROPIA. El derecho, interés o deseo de uno. (v. Nombre.propio [En].) PUBLICA. La
utilidad o el bien general. El interés de la patria. La conveniencia de los más sin olvido de los menos. SIMULADA. La presentada como verdadera por las partes, sin tener en sí existencia real.

spanishDefinition:
En el procedimiento criminal se llaman indicios, modo que conduzcan lógica y naturalmente al hecho de que se trata; que sean concordantes los unos con los otros de manera que tengan íntima conexión entre sí y se relacionen sin esfuerzo, desde el punto de partida hasta el fin buscado, y que se funden en hechos reales y probados, nunca en otras presunciones o indicios. Estos son los requisitos exigidos por la legislación predominante. y también presunciones, las circunstancias y antecedentes que, teniendo relación con el delito, pueden razonablemente fundar una opinión sobre hechos determinados. Así, pues, el indicio constituye un medio probatorio conocido como “prueba indiciaria”. Puede decirse que generalmente los indicios abren el camino a la investigación de los delitos. Unos muebles volcados, la posición de la víctima, la marca de un pie o una mano, la ceniza de un cigarro, un trozo de tela son elementos que, técnicamente examinados, pueden orientar sobre el posible móvil, el momento de la comisión y acerca del
autor. Tienen, por lo tanto, un extraordinario valor en criminalística, y, unidos a otras pruebas, sirven al juzgador para establecer un juicio definitivo. A veces, los indicios hacen por sí solos plena prueba, siempre que el cuerpo del delito conste por pruebas directas e inmediatas; que sean varios, reuniendo, cuando menos, el carácter de anteriores al hecho y concomitantes con él; que se relacionen con el hecho primordial que debe servir de punto de partida para la conclusión que se busca; que sean directos, de modo que conduzcan lógica y naturalmente al hecho de que se trata; que sean concordantes los unos con los otros de manera que tengan íntima conexión entre sí y se relacionen sin esfuerzo, desde el punto de partida hasta el fin buscado, y que se funden en hechos reales y

englishDefinition:
1. Criminal law. A reasonable ground to suspect that a person has committed or is committing a crime or that a place contains specific items connected with a crime.• Under the Fourth Amendment, probable cause - which amounts to more than a bare suspicion but less than evidence that would justify a conviction must be shown before an
arrest warrant or search warrant may be issued. Also termed reasonable cause; sufficient cause; reasonable grounds; reasonable excuse Cf. reasonable suspicion
under SUSPICION. [Cases: Arrest C=>63.4(2).] "Probable cause may not be established simply by showing that the officer who made the challenged arrest or search
subjectively believed he had grounds for his action. As emphasized in Beck v. Ohio [379 U.S. 89, 85 S.Ct. 223 (1964)J: 'If subjective good faith alone were the test, the
protection of the Fourth Amendment would evaporate, and the people would be "secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects" only in the discretion of the police.'
The probable cause test, then, is an objective one; for there to be probable cause, the facts must be such as would warrant a belief by a reasonable man." Wayne R. LaFave
& Jerold H. Israel. Criminal Procedure § 3.3, at 140 (2d ed.1992).
2. Torts. A reasonable belief in the existence of facts on which a claim is based and in the legal validity of the claim itself.• In this sense, probable cause is usu. assessed as of the time when the claimant brings the claim (as by filing suit). 3. A reasonable basis to support issuance of an administrative warrant based on either (1) specific evidence of an existing violation of administrative rules, or (2) evidence showing that a particular business meets the legislative or administrative standards permitting an inspection ofthe business premises. [Cases: Searches and Seizures ~129.]

english: There is a wealth of criminal terminology in Spanish and in English relating to sex crimes, partially due to the fact that the criminality or non-criminality of certain acts has changed over time, and also due to changes in the way that societies, both Anglo and Hispanic, have decided to describe the crimes. Specifically, there has been a strong movement in the last half-century or so to make sex crimes less "morally" described (ofensas contra el honor, el pudor, p.ej.), and more clinically descriptive. This has led to the reclassification in many countries of sex crimes into either 'abuso' or 'agresión' (abuse/assuault). The differentiating factor between the two is, often, whether or not there was resistance on the part of the victim, or violence on the part of the aggressor. There were high-profile cases in Spain in 2019 which threw the inherent difficulty of this classification into relief, wherein women who were semi-conscious or unconscious due to drugs or alcohol, and therefore did not resist, were considered to be victims of abuse, rather than assault.
source: Refactor_ EOIR Spanish-English Glossary 2020.xlsx - Sex Crimes.csv

comments: The usage of terms surrounding these concepts is very messy: people use a number of terms interchangeably, or sometimes with different meanings that aren't necessarily standardized. You might think that 'public benefits' would refer, specifically, to state funded healthcare, but many people use it interchangeably with 'public assistance', which can (and does) refer to monies received by persons who for whatever reason need financial assistance. 'Public assistance' can also refer to monies provided by the government to help develop certain industrial sectors, or small business loans (this, in Spain, is also referred to as ayudas públicas, so at least the ambiguity and confusion exist in both languages). When interpreting, do your best to match the specificity or vagueness of the source, and don't be afraid to use Spanglish or US usage ('beneficios', 'aseguranza médica'). After all, in many Spanish-speaking countries, publicly-funded healthcare is the norm, and so asking someone 'sus hijos tienen la sanidad pública?' might not make a lot of sense, especially in the US context.
